Aetius
ā-ē´shĭ-ŭs
n. (Aetius of Antioch, d. c. 367, deacon and dialectician, founder of the extreme Arian party called Anomoean, nicknamed the Atheist)
Greek Aetios, from aetos, an eagle. His opponents called him ho atheos, the godless, for the consequence of his doctrine.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Aetius rose from a goldsmith's bench to be the sharpest logician of the Arian cause, and he is the teacher behind Eunomius. He was ordained deacon at Antioch and set himself to prove by syllogism that the Son is anomoios — unlike the Father — publishing three hundred short propositions to that end. His method was pure Aristotelian dialectic applied to the being of God: define the Father as the Unbegotten, observe that the Son is begotten, and conclude a difference of essence. The orthodox did not answer him chiefly by better logic but by Scripture and by naming the method itself as the error. Col 2:8 stands over his whole career: “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men.” So does 1Ti 6:20, with its warning against “oppositions of science falsely so called.” Aetius was deposed, exiled under Constantius, briefly restored under Julian the Apostate, and died without a church. He is remembered because he shows what the Arian premise becomes when a fearless man follows it all the way down: not a lower Christ, but no Christ at all.

Webster 1828 Definition

Key Scripture

Col 2:8 — "Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ."

1Co 1:20 — "Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?"

Pro 3:5 — "Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding."

1Ti 6:20 — "O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called:"

Modern Corruption

Aetius is the standing proof that a method may be rigorous and its conclusion blasphemous, and that reason set over revelation does not stay neutral.

expand to see more

The error in Aetius is not that he reasoned but that he made reason the judge of what God has said. Given his definitions his syllogisms were tight; the definitions were the heresy. This is the permanent temptation of the theological academy, and it is why Pro 3:5 says “lean not unto thine own understanding” in the same breath as it commands trust with the whole heart. Scripture does not forbid logic; it forbids logic enthroned. The same move is made today whenever a doctrine plainly taught is rejected because it will not reduce to a syllogism the reasoner already accepts.

The second corruption is the respectability his kind of rigour still buys. Aetius was admired for his acuteness while he was emptying the Godhead, and the church has repeatedly mistaken sharpness for soundness. 1Co 1:20 asks “where is the disputer of this world?” and answers that God has made foolish the wisdom of this world. The recovery is to test the conclusion by the Word and not the Word by the conclusion, and to hold that the Son is of one substance with the Father because Scripture reveals it, whatever a man's definitions require.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek philosophia (G5385), love of wisdom; suzetetes (G4804), a disputer; gnosis (G1108), knowledge.

Greek philosophia (G5385) — philosophy, used in warning; Colossians 2:8.

Greek suzetetes (G4804) — a disputer, a debater; 1 Corinthians 1:20.

Greek gnosis (G1108) — knowledge, the science falsely so called; 1 Timothy 6:20.

Greek kenophonia (G2757) — vain babbling, empty sound; 1 Timothy 6:20.

Hebrew binah (H998) — understanding, not to be leaned upon; Proverbs 3:5.

Usage

"“Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit” (Col 2:8) — the verse his career illustrates."

"“where is the disputer of this world?” (1Co 1:20) — the question put to his acuteness."

"“oppositions of science falsely so called” (1Ti 6:20) — his three hundred propositions named."
